**About this position**
-----------------------


Do you want to contribute to the energy transition by analysing how Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and large nuclear reactors can be integrated into a congested, renewable\-heavy power grid?


SMRs are increasingly recognised as a promising technology to support reliable, low\-carbon energy systems. Unlike conventional large nuclear power plants, SMRs offer greater operational flexibility and can adapt their electricity and heat output to changing system conditions. This flexibility allows nuclear generation to complement intermittent renewable sources such as wind and solar, while contributing to grid stability and industrial decarbonisation.


As new nuclear capacity is added to the grid, understanding its interaction with network constraints becomes essential. Nuclear generation, in both baseload and flexible modes, can influence congestion patterns, system stability, and the need for network reinforcements. Through capabilities such as load\-following, frequency regulation, and voltage support, nuclear plants can help manage congestion and stabilise prices, particularly when coupled with storage or hydrogen production. Mapping these effects at the high\-voltage level, and comparing how SMRs and large reactors each perform under different grid and market conditions, is a key step towards designing a robust nuclear deployment strategy.


**What will be your role?**
---------------------------


In this internship/thesis project, you will investigate how SMRs and large nuclear reactors can be integrated into the future electricity grid, with a focus on grid congestion management and system\-level value. Your work will combine power\-system analysis with the flexibility characteristics of nuclear generation.


You will explore how nuclear plants can provide flexibility services, load\-following, frequency and voltage support, while interacting with renewable generation, electrification, and industrial energy demand. Particular attention will be given to grid


congestion in key regions and to the role of nuclear in supporting the electrification of industrial clusters such as the Rotterdam area.


The project will include one or more of the following research directions:


* Mapping grid congestion patterns and identifying bottlenecks at the high\-voltage level;
* Assessing the impact of nuclear operation (baseload and flexible modes) on congestion management and system stability;
* Evaluating required network reinforcements and associated investments under different scenarios;
* Analysing the interaction between nuclear, renewables, electrification, hydrogen, and storage;
* Simulating market dispatch under network constraints and assessing price formation, congestion effects, and the operational value of flexibility;
* Comparing the system value and flexibility contributions of SMRs versus large reactors, and the conditions under which each technology performs optimally.

**About this position**
With the evolution of cellular networks, radio access network (RAN) complexity is continuously increasing. The explosive use of AI in recent times, as well as services like extended reality (XR) and the continuous use of video streaming services, are projected to significantly increase the demand for radio resource capacity in 6G networks. Therefore, for network mobile operators, it is critical to be able to monitor and/or forecast spatiotemporal traffic evolutions and take appropriate and timely actions (e.g. deploy additional base stations/antennas, adopt new technological solutions or change the network configuration) to ensure that the network can deliver all services at all times. This graduation project focuses on developing a decision support system (DSS) to autonomously manage the 6G RAN. Thus, the DSS is responsible for performing traffic predictions, predicting potential performance issues, analysing candidate solutions to prevent the predicted performance issues, and provide timely recommendations to the operator on which action to take. The operation of the DSS will be based on the use of a network digital twin (NDT), which will provide the replica of the real network and will allow the evaluation of the various candidate solutions. Moreover, additional automation for the DSS can be achieved by AI agents, which can reason, plan, and take actions. These AI agents can be leveraged for multiple functionalities such as traffic prediction, building/configuring the NDT, recommend candidate solutions for evaluation, and interpret the NDT evaluations.
